title: Spatial scale space from hemigroup axioms: the theory of image pyramids
description:
An image pyramid smooths and subsamples an image by a fixed ratio q at every level. The classical design literature constrains the kernel of one step and follows the equivalent kernels that the pyramid builds level by level. Scale-space theory has a kernel at every scale and leaves the subsampling outside its treatment. This paper studies kernel families on ℝ^d under the hemigroup axioms of linear scale space, in which two consecutive smoothing steps compose to one, with covariance under the powers of q in place of every dilation. It gives a description of the families by their data, a selection theorem and an obstruction on the grid. The isotropic families form three nested strata: all of them, those covariant under the powers of q, and those covariant under every dilation. In the middle stratum the kernel from the scale 0 to each scale is semi-selfdecomposable: it is its own contraction by q, smoothed by an infinitely divisible law. The scales are labelled so that dilating the kernel at a scale t by q gives the kernel at qt, and an octave step goes from t to qt. The ladder of octave steps between the stored levels determines the kernels at the knots q^n. No law of bounded support other than a point mass is a step of any family that obeys the cascade and is continuous in scale. Every octave step of the pyramid is one implicit heat step, a Helmholtz resolvent, and the pyramid is covariant under every dilation. Up to a relabelling g of the scales with g(qt) = q g(t), it is the one isotropic family covariant under q whose octave steps from every scale obey the maximum principle of an implicit Euler step for every smooth rapidly decreasing input. Among symmetric rotation-invariant laws the principle holds exactly for the Helmholtz resolvents, so Gaussian steps fail it. The principle is required of the octave steps only. A step of the pyramid has it only across a factor q in scale, and no symmetric family has it at every step. A grid pyramid applies one mask, a probability law, at every level, and it is called exact when the steps it applies from level to level are the octave steps of one family continuous in scale and covariant under q. On a lattice, a symmetric probability mask other than a point mass has an exact grid pyramid if and only if it is infinitely divisible with a logarithmic moment. For laws the sufficiency is a theorem of Maejima and Ueda, and continuity in scale gives the necessity. For an integer ratio the kernels of an exact grid pyramid on hℤ^d are singular. In d ≥ 2 no kernel at a positive scale of an exact grid pyramid whose mask is carried by a lattice is rotation invariant. The same holds when the dilation is an invertible matrix, which may also turn the lattice. The obstruction needs continuity in scale: some band-limited mask w of infinite support has a rotation-invariant law μ with D_qμ = μ * w. The lemmas, propositions and theorems of Sections 3 to 6 and of the supplement have formal counterparts in Lean 4. All are machine-checked but one step and three results proved in print only, in whole or in part: the proposition on matrix dilations, the singularity clause on the kernels, and the band-limited example. The formal counterparts rest on nine cited facts, taken as fourteen axioms that the supplement prints in Lean, and on two earlier formal developments of the author's. One of the nine is a proposition of an earlier paper of the author's that restates a theorem of Karlin. Neither the connecting prose nor the numerical examples are machine-checked, and the formal statements and definitions were compared with the printed ones by AI agents only.

This deposit is the article's verification export: the PDF, its LaTeX source, the Lean 4 modules its statements rest on, the trust boundary with the ledger of cited facts, the blueprint chapters, the process account and the external reviews.
